description: Square-section prestressed concrete post with a short steel bracket arm and a cobra-head lantern

image.prompt:
Product photograph of one isolated object, shot from a HIGH THREE-QUARTER ANGLE: the camera is well above the object and tilted down about 30 degrees, so the top of the object is clearly visible along with its front and one side. Not a straight-on elevation.

The object: Tall precast concrete post, square in section and tapering slightly as it rises straight out of the ground with no base plate, its faces carrying a regular column of small round cast holes down the shaft, the top of the post finished flat, and clamped near the top a short straight steel bracket arm angling up and out to one side carrying a closed cobra-head lantern housing shaped as a broad wedge that tapers to a shallow rounded nose with a flat clear lens panel underneath Materials: Grey precast concrete with a coarse mottled surface, dark water staining and algae greening up the lowest two metres, rust bleeding from the cast holes and the bracket clamp, chipped arrises exposing pale aggregate, painted lantern housing chalky and sun-faded.

Form: build the object from a few simple, chunky, closed volumes. Prefer solid panels over lattice, mesh, grilles or perforated screens; keep any openings few, large and clearly separated. No thin spindly protrusions, no wires, no chains, no fringes, no lace, no fine filigree, no dense repeated slots or cut-outs. Keep the silhouette simple and readable from every side. Keep the object's SHAPE simple; richness must come from the surface finish, wear and materials rather than from intricate geometry. The object is still photoreal and highly detailed in its texture -- only its form is simple.

Framing: long-lens near-orthographic perspective, minimal foreshortening. The object is perfectly centred and occupies about 75% of the frame height, with clear empty margin on all four sides. The whole object is in frame; nothing is cropped.

Background: completely flat seamless pure WHITE studio matte. The object floats in empty space against an infinite seamless white backdrop, photographed as a cut-out with nothing underneath it. There is no surface for it to rest on and nothing for it to cast a shadow onto. No floor, no ground plane, no horizon line, no cast shadow, no contact shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient. This is a studio cut-out, NOT an outdoor photograph: there must be no sky, no clouds, no buildings, no road and no overhead cables anywhere in the frame.

Lighting: flat even studio illumination from all sides, soft and shadowless, like a lightbox. No strong key light, no rim light, no coloured light, no specular blowout, no dramatic highlights. Colours must read as true albedo. The lamp is switched OFF and emits no light.

One object only, nothing else in frame. No people, no hands, no other props, no packaging, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows, no borders, no drop shadow.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, clean and undamaged geometry, realistic materials and surface wear. Not stylised, not cartoon, not low-poly, not a 3D render preview, not a wireframe.

license.notice: Fully synthetic. No third-party scanned or scraped geometry.

review.critique: Final measured cost against all four ceilings. Measured bbox 1.688 x 8.0 x 0.29 m. Cost: 468 triangles / 16000, 4 draw calls / 12, 4 materials / 8, 4 unique geometries / 16, 1 textures. Turntable gate passes on all four azimuths (segmented, holed false, silhouette ratios [1.0, 0.765, 0.991, 0.9], interior hole fractions [0.0001, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]).  Four components at 4 draw calls, 4 materials and 4 geometries against a hero2x ceiling of 12/8/16 -- the tapered square pole is 12 triangles as one frustum, which is what leaves the holes and bracket gear affordable.

featureReviews.notes: Measured bbox 1.688 x 8.000 x 0.290 m against the declared 1.7 x 8 x 0.3 -- within 1% on width and height and 3% on depth. Width is the 1.5 m bracket reach plus the shaft, exactly as the asset notes describe it. Proportion comes from the DECLARATION: silh.mjs puts the plate's subject at 396 x 904 px, which at 8 m tall would imply a 3.50 m width.

A tapered SQUARE frustum, 0.215 m at the foot to 0.135 m at the top, with a chamfered cap and thirteen recessed cast holes down one face between 1.10 and 6.60 m. The previous build was a smooth round cylinder with none of it, against asset notes that call the holes identity-defining. The whole shaft is 12 triangles as one frustum, which is what left room for the holes and the bracket gear to be real geometry.

Two steel BANDS wrapping the pole 22 mm proud of its faces, a 1.40 m arm off the upper one, and a diagonal strut from the lower band up to mid-arm. The strut matters: without it the arm reads as floating off the pole, and the plate shows it clearly. There is no cast boss and no bolt flange on the real thing -- the clamp is the whole reason this is a lamp bolted to an ordinary distribution pole rather than a purpose-made column.

A three-box cast wedge tapering from a 0.29 m spigot to a 0.22 m nose over an acrylic refractor bowl hung proud of the casting. Its depth is what sets the declared 0.30 m envelope depth -- at 0.23 the measured bbox came in 23% under. Not carried: the plate's lantern is tilted nose-down and mine is level, which is a real difference and is why this is 0.90 rather than higher.

Four material layers: weathered concrete #9d9c94 measured off the plate's subject mask (p25 106,106,98 / p50 127,126,121 / p75 167,164,149), rusted bracket steel #8b8378 at metalness 0.30 -- painted and rusting rather than hot-dipped, unlike the galvanised columns elsewhere in this kit -- cast aluminium #a8adad and acrylic #d6dad4. Luma 126 is clear of the 55.5-60.5 band gatecrop's alpha key erases, so no lift was needed.

Green algae over the bottom 3 m as an axis tint MULTIPLIED into the concrete rather than a second material, which is what the plate shows -- strongest at the foot and gone by about 3 m. Pale spalled patches where the surface has broken to the aggregate ride on the same material as a post-construction canvas tile. What is NOT carried is the plate's rust bleed running down from the clamp, which is directional and the tile is isotropic.

name: Concrete Street Lamp Column
nameTh: เสาไฟฟ้าคอนกรีตพร้อมโคม
notes:
The cheap provincial and secondary-road standard: the lamp is clamped to an ordinary prestressed concrete pole rather than a purpose-made steel column, so it reads as concrete first and lamp second. Width is the 1.5 m bracket reach plus the shaft; the post itself is about 0.2 m square at the base. The cast holes down the shaft are real -- they are the lifting and fixing holes in a spun-and-cast Thai pole and are the fastest way to tell it from a plain concrete bollard at distance. budgetClass pinned to hero against the hero2x its 8 m height would derive, because the prop is one tapered box, one bracket and one lantern, and these are placed in long runs where 16k triangles and 12 draw calls each would dominate the frame. Static: cast into the ground, so physics stays disabled.

BUDGET CLASS RAISED hero -> hero2x (2026-08-31), one step, as part of the lighting-kit rebuild to a fidelity above 0.92. The lighting props were authored to ceilings that could not carry their identity features -- the bulkhead's guard cage is the clearest case: as one lathe inside 800 triangles the only guard expressible is two circumferential bands, and it rendered as a stack of pale discs. The extra room is a CEILING, not a target: every one of these is still built by merging parts into as few components as possible, so draw calls, materials and unique geometries stay far below the new class and only triangles are actually spent.
